don't let my steam "hours played" metric deceive you: KOF 98 is a game I played for 2-3 hours a day, every day, for months after I first got my hands on it. It was a game with 56 playable characters -a ridiculous amount at the time, even more so today - and I made it my business to get to know them all. By the end I could play a team at random and have a decent chance at pulling out a victory against my friends.
KOF 98 Ultimate Match takes that core gem, that timeless classic, and throws in even more characters. So now there's no need to ask about your fav because your fav is RETROACTIVELY IN THE GAME (unless your fav is K9999, sorry)
I admit I'm smitten and old and my perspective is hardly universal: if you're new to KOF or fighting games in general, this is a lot to absorb. And the game's tutorials/challenges are terrible at explaining just what the hell is going on or what you need to learn. But if you can find your way into this game it can give you an infinite amount of replayability. And SNK packed this game with so many colorful personalities that I promise you that you'll fall in love with at least one character who may or may not be named Yamazaki.

KOF '98. A classic fighting game with not a lot of bloat. Sure, the roster's big, but it's also a celebration of KOF so we can let that slide, yeah? Besides, who doesn't love having so many options? The original game was missing 7 characters, however (or 9 if you count Orochi Iori and Leona). Couldn't even play the boss in arcades. Ultimate Match remedies the cut character problem, and adds a slew of new alternate movesets for many characters (hold Select while choosing). Also features a challenge mode, but there's little substance to it. It may teach you mildly advanced techniques, however! All in all, Ultimate Match is the definitive '98 experience. And hey, the online play has rollback.

'98 UMFE is way more accessible than 2002UM:
The first thing I noticed was that jump-ins into C or D are actually not too hard. Except that you'll still have to confirm the jump-in (and/or input the super) [i]extremely[/i] quickly.
Max Mode is way more comprehensible, being used as a way to end your combos with a buffed super or just as a general increase of damage and pushback. The latter makes it so that combos will be harder, but good pokes, zoning or knockback attacks will yield more reward on hit.
Having step dash (available in Extra or Ultimate Mode) increases your walk speed to 130%, making max mode footsies a lot of fun.

There are some minor inconveniences, like the record function requiring a second input device.

If you can't get the PS2, or any CD version of this game, here's the best next alternative honestly. At least there's online to make up for it...but beware of the high ping spikes. Don't just match with anyone. Make sure you check their ping and that it's around 100 and below before you go into a match. I've had very laggy matches due to ignoring the ping at first, and then very awesome matches because I paid attention to the ping.

If you are getting the game to play online with friends...hopefully you won't experience ping problems with them. Otherwise, search for a player you could rival up against, friend them, and play away! A great experience and good training!

Now as for the game itself. King of Fighters 98 is a much more simplified game than what it became with XIII and even 2002. You'll be using more basic combos, some juggles, and technical gameplay strategies to outwit your opponents with mix-ups and what not.

There's a great selection of characters and they all play very unique from one another. Not to mention, there are even second versions of some characters usually based on previous renditions of them whether it's referenced to older KoF games or their origin (such as Fatal Fury or Art of Fighting.)

Unfortunately, why I reccommend to get the a CD based version, (Neo geo cd, PS2, etc) is for its incredible arranged soundtrack, color edit (I enjoy this since it allows me to personalize my main team), and actually functional graphic filters.

Let's just hope they patch a whatever they can with the netcode, and maybe that someone will make a mod to add in the Arranged sountrack.

Otherwise, I'd still reccommend the game to anyone who wants a taste of King of Fighters' origins beign that people claim this is the most balanced KoF game. Definitely worth it for Fighting gamers!

The consensus is that this is the best game in the series; and I would not disagree with that statement.  If you have played any of the older KOF games(pre PS3/XBOX360), then this game will be familiar territory.  The game has a solid roster, good game play, and doesn't get too complex with it's bars/meters. Overall, it is a very solid fighting game.  As for this edition, there are several changes.  First, there are additional characters added since the original arcade version including several boss characters from past games.  Second, some of the characters received new or modified moves and (S)DMs.  Third, there is an inclusion of a 3rd mode that is included which is customizable from a combination of extra and advanced modes.  As for online, there isn't a lot of people playing the game so finding a match can be challenging.  However, overall, this is a solid game, and for any fan, it should be a must buy.

In summary, if you are a KOF fan, I absolutely recommend this game, but likely, you've already purchased it.  If you are a fighting game fan in general, or would like to get into the series, this is definitely a recommended title.

This is the final rendition of one of the best 2D fighting games of all time. The balance has been re-tweeked, several characters have been added and now there is online play (welcome to 2005). 
The graphics are certainly of the nostalgic variety; if you enjoy the old school sprites of yesteryear, you will feel right at home. If you aren't a fan of that retro look, the game still moves and plays silky smooth and decently quick. 

A gamepad is a minimum requirement for this game, so if you don't already have one, that extra investment is to be considered. To truly experience this game to its full potential, I strongly suggest purchasing a fightstick. This game is fully playable with a keyboard, and some actually do, but it is not recommended.

Now let's talk a bit about the online. Quite frankly, the online in this game is acceptable. I know several people lombast it, but compared to other fighting games, it certainly isn't bad. As the title shows, [i]The King of Fighters ’98: Ultimate Match ~Final Edition~[/i] is the last revision of the game that was originally released on Taito Type X arcades and the PlayStation 2. [i]Ultimate Match[/i] is a remake of the original [i]The King of Fighters ’98: The Slugfest[/i] ([i]Dream Match Never Ends[/i] in Japan) which was released in 1998 for both the Neo Geo AES (console) and MVS (arcade). This version of the game is also included, so players are able to see what changed between the two versions. The Final Edition version also made further changes to some characters in Ultimate Match for balance purposes. The Gallery Mode and Color Edit mode from the PS2 version are not present though, but that is not a major loss.

The original [i]KOF ‘98[/i] didn’t have a plot, SNK instead choose to include almost every character that had appeared in previous games in a so-called “Dream Match”. As the fifth KOF game, this was probably considered a milestone and they wanted to celebrate (the series’ plot would be continued with the next game and characters that had been killed in previous games would not appear, unless it was for fan service). The original KOF ’98 had 51 characters (including extra or alternate versions) and Ultimate Match adds more characters, effectively making sure that every character that appeared in a prior KOF game is present. [b]Eiji[/b] from KOF ’95 and [b]Kasumi[/b] from KOF ’96 (both characters from the [i]Art of Fighting[/i] series) are now Edit Characters and the Boss Team from KOF ’96 (made of [b]Geese[/b], [b]Krauser[/b] and [b]Mr. Big[/b]) is included. Additionally, the final bosses of KOF ’96 and KOF ’97, [b]Goenitz[/b] and [b]Orochi[/b] respectively, are included in the game (and in this version are playable from the start) alongside the mid-bosses from KOF ’97, the Orochi versions of [b]Leona[/b] and [b]Iori[/b]. Together with alternate versions of Geese, [b]Blue Mary[/b] and [b]Yamazaki[/b], the total number of characters increases to 64. The characters were rebalanced for Ultimate Match, and Final Edition makes further changes to the characters to level the competitive balance.

The game features two different modes of play: the traditional KOF arcade play and single play, which has a total of seven stages. In the former, players use a team of three fighters and instead of a round system, the winning team is the one that eliminates all of their opponents. Single Play uses a traditional system of rounds. A second player can join in at any time during arcade play, but there is a separate mode for two players. A separate mode allows a single player to play against the CPU for as long as they want without the arcade mode progression. The game includes an Endless Mode, which is a survival mode in which the player tries to defeat as much opponents as possible using a single character until they are defeated (the original game has a Survivor Mode, in which the player uses a single character to defeat all other characters, a combination of a Survival and Time Attack mode). The game also has a robust Practice Mode with the same options that were introduced in the PS2 version of [i]The King of Fighters 2003[/i]. Finally, the game has Online Play, which allows players to perform quick and custom matches in Player or Ranked matches.

The gameplay of the KOF series is an extension of what started with the [i]Fatal Fury[/i] and the Art of Fighting series, mostly the former. There are four attack buttons, two punches and two kicks, light and strong. Pressing both light buttons at the same time will make the character use a dodge maneuver while pressing both strong buttons will have them perform a strong attack that always knocks down the opponent. Each character has a variety of throws and special moves, as well as unique command attacks. Characters also have super moves, known as Desperation Moves (DM), which are done by using a super meter. Before selecting their characters, players need to select between three systems that determine their dash style, their dodging maneuver and how their power meter is used. Two of these systems debuted in KOF ’97 and were also used in KOF ’98, [b]Advanced[/b] and [b]Extra[/b]. Most fighting game players will probably recognize these systems from [i]Capcom Vs. SNK 2: Mark of the Millennium 2001[/i] as the N Groove and the S Groove respectively. Advanced was a new system first introduced in KOF ’97 that uses stocks. Using special moves, players can fill this meter and once full, they gain a stock which can be used to perform a DM or activate MAX mode (by pressing both punch buttons and the light kick button at the same time) to perform a Super Desperation Move. In this mode characters can roll forward or backward as a dodge maneuver and they can run by double tapping the directional pad towards their opponent.

The system used in Extra is the one that was first introduced in KOF ’94 and was used last in this game. Instead of running, the character makes a small hop forward, and instead of being able to roll, the character dodges into the background. While dodging, the character is able to attack (this could be done in [i]Fatal Fury 2[/i] and [i]Special[/i], but the character had to block). The super meter can be filled manually by the player by pressing the same three buttons to activate MAX Mode in Advanced, though it also increases when they take damage. In Ultimate Match, Extra Mode has a single stock which allows for MAX activation as well. When the character’s health is low, players can perform Desperation Moves even when their meter is not full, though an interval has been added in this version to ensure players do not spam the moves. Super Desperation Moves can be performed with the same requirements from Advanced Mode in this version, or with a combination of a full meter and low health.

The final system is exclusive to Ultimate Match and is appropriately named [b]Ultimate[/b]. This mode allows players to select a setting that fits their play style or a character’s fighting style. They can choose their running style, what dodge move they can perform and what super meter properties to have. This will also give the characters the inherent properties and systems of the chosen subsystem. Now that the controls and systems are out of the way, I guess I should write about the fighting. I’ll assume that people who read this review are familiar with other 2D fighters such as the [i]Street Fighter[/i] series and other KOF games, both previous and later ones.

One unique aspect of fighting in KOF is the jumping; the game has four different types of jumps, two which are unique to KOF. These two are the Short Hop and the Hyper Hop (they have many other names as well, but I will be using these here). Players can make their characters hop both forward and backward. These hops increase the pace of the game by keeping players on the offensive. Players who want to get into KOF need to learn and become acquainted with these jumping techniques and how to counter them in order to do well in the game, since they will be using them constantly both to poke their opponents and defend themselves using normal attacks, and also to perform cross-ups. The other two jumps are the normal jump and the Super Jump, these last one, like the Hyper Hop, can be done while running.

KOF ’98 is considered by many to be the best in the series (opinions changed somewhat after players got to play [i]The King of Fighters XIII[/i], but [i]The King of Fighters XI[/i] is officially the secret best KOF), so it is the perfect game to start with the series if players have never played any KOF games before. Players that love to play 2D fighters need to play this game, along with the aforementioned XIII, XI and [i]The King of Fighters 2002: Unlimited Match[/i]. The best way to appreciate the fighting game genre is to play as many of its games as possible, and the KOF games are among the best in it.

"The King of Fighters '98 - Dream Match Never Ends/The Slugfest" is one of those games that never get old (and get even better as they get older). Great roster of fighters, excellent art and almost-unmatched gameplay makes an unforgettable fighting experience! Its graphics and visual effects continue to be impressive even almost twenty years later, with beautifully-animated sprites and rich backgrounds, accompanied by superb voice acting and some of the loudest sound effects I've ever heard.

As this is a "dream match"-style game, released after the conclusion of the Orochi story arc, there isn't much to say story-wise; it features most of the characters which appeared from KOF '94 to '97, Rugal returning as the final boss (using his "Omega" form), and the "Ultimate Match" version has additional characters, such as the Boss Team and Eiji Kisaragi, among others. Ultimate Match also adds new backgrounds, along with a new fighting style, "Ultimate".

KOF'98 still keeps itself fresh, exciting and relevant after all those years. Its competitive potential is enough to keep players hooked for hours, fighting against each other, and the computer-controlled fighters can also pose a great challenge for those who prefer to spend their time playing by themselves. However, its matchmaking service is lacking (well, at least it does not seem to work as it should here; maybe it's a connection issue) and online battles are plagued with delay, rendering the game almost unplayable sometimes. I wish there were more players available for online matches, nonetheless.

The King of FIghters series is aptly named as to date it's still my favourite fighting series. It's technical, flashy and oozes style and KoF 98 is the absolute cream of the crop. This Steam version is in my opinion the optimal version of KoF 98 as it combines many of the best elements of previous versions, my only complaint is it would have been nice to have included the arranged soundtrack as an option, but that said the original soundtrack is still spectacular.

So what makes KoF so good? For one I really like the story of these games which I realise is an unusual pro for a fighting game series, but from Fatal Fury (technically the first KoF) I found myself invested in the characters, specifically Terry Bogard's grudge match with Geese Howard and their battle across South Town and my interest has only grown from there. KoF's roster is large and loud, boasting unique personalities that all have their own reasons for entering the tournament and have interesting and sometimes comical pre fight interactions with one another. Once again as with many Neo Geo titles SNK really pushed the hardware at the time and worked within it's limitations to truly create something special, it's a delight to play and it looks fantastic. From the introduction sequence you'll instantly pick up the visual style and fantastic sound direction, intro sequences in arcade games are usually something special as they lure in punters to spend their hard earned cash and here it's no exception, the opening theme and video effects really get you in the mood for a good scrap. Starting up the game here you pick your style and three fighters to roll with, you can opt to go with the pre selected teams or mix and match to create your own unique one, this can be a little daunting for new players as it means you have to learn three characters if you want to get good and play competitively against others, but if you have the patience to put in the time it really pays off.

I'm not sure what else to say, if you're a fighting game fanatic you no doubt already have your own opinions on KoF 98, if you're a newcomer there are maybe easier places to start, but don't let that discourage you, because if you really put in the time you'll have a handle on one of the greatest fighting games of all time. So what are you waiting for, grab an arcade stick, choose your fighters and get ready for the greatest smack down of your life!

I had some reservations at first about whether the changes added to KOF '98 warranted its rerelease and sale price. After some time with it, it's become clear that this tweaked and expanded version truly is a worthy update to one of the best fighting games ever made. A handful of new characters expand the roster a bit, but the addition of a significant amount of alternate versions of both pre-existing and new characters really beef up your options for team creation nicely. The changes are rounded out by a slight rebalance, the addition of a new mode to Advanced and EX, and online matchmaking. Throwing in the original version as well was a nice touch. Most of the criticism leveled at this game seems to come from the fact that it's not the PS2 version. This is still one of the most rock-solid fighting games in existence, with or without a few cosmetic bells and whistles, the absence of which hardly justifies a negative review. It's colorful, balanced, charming, fun, and accessible. If you're new to KOF and cut your teeth on XIII, pick this one up and get a taste of fighting's golden age; There's a good chance you'll find this game superior to its later installments. If you're a Neo Geo veteran, you'll come to enjoy the changes even if you're a hardened purist.

Ah, KOF '98... One of the all-time greats of the fighting game genre,
and now, you got it here on steam at a much more affordable price than what I had to shell out for a Neo Geo CDZ, it even has online play to boot! So if you like fighters and wanted to check out KOF, make it this one.

The roster is made up of every single fighter featured from KOF '94 to '97
with the last couple of missing combatants being additions for the "Ultimate Match" update from some years back.

You got two different styles, or "Grooves" if you are so inclined.
Advanced plays like your average KOF game today, you fill up your gauge by fighting and it eventually adds up into separate stocks. Using a special move consumes one stock, but you can also use a stock to enter a super mode, from there, you can use one more stock to do your character's most powerful move, The other mode on the other hand takes after KOF '94-'96's style with you having to charge your stocks manually and being granted the ability to use infinite supers when at low health. The rest of the gameplay follows a 3-man team-based structure, though you cannot tag in and out party members. Once all your characters are exhausted, you lose. 
By far the most striking feature of KOF, however, is the jumping mechanics.
You got several different types of jumping at your disposal, like a short hop and another, entirely different hyper-hop that advances you forward quickly while still staying low to the ground. I only occassionally play it compared to KoF XIII's solid mechanics and KoF 2002's insane roster of characters but KoF98 has a lot of little charms that are missing from the latter games. The stages are more characterful and change between bouts with all sorts of little details hidden away that they didn't seem to bother with in the later games. There's a lot more character interactions before the start of rounds which is an excellent way of fleshing out who these characters are and how they relate to one another without resorting to sometimes lengthly dialogue excahnages as you get in KoF XIII and Blazblue. It's probably the toughest of the KoF games on Steam and because of it's multiple systems, has a lot more depth to it but it also has some of the most overpowered characters as well (Orochi in particular). 

The bottom line: If you're a casual fighting fan like me then KoF 98 offers a good roster of characters and some of the best visual design in the genre (which is why I like it) but KoF XIII is generally prettier and a lot easier to get into.

Back in 1998, this was the most anticipated title after the thrilling conclusion of the Orochi saga as seen in the King of Fighters 97. Although this title lacked any sort of story at all, it made up for it with the inclusion of all characters seen up to that point including those had been retired or killed during the story, as well as an overall improvement in gameplay speed & balance.

Which explains the lack of extras such as reworked 3D stages & an arranged soundtrack that were featured in home versions such as the one released for the Playstation 2 at the time. But do not let the lack of those extras discourage you from playing this excellent title. Featuring perhaps the largest roster seen in the series thus far, you may rest assured that you are certain to find characters that suit your playing style.

All in all, this is a highly recommended title for KOF fans that may have missed the second revision of the game back at the arcades, as well as younger fighting game fans who have an interest in old-school fighting games.

Usually, one shouldn't fix what isn't broke, but sometimes it doesn't hurt to do so.  KOF98 Ultimate Match is one of those times.

An updated version of the classic Neo-Geo 3-on-3 fighting game, Ultimate Match provides players with a truly complete roster of characters from the first three KOF games.  The conspicuously absent Boss Team from 1996 joins the game roster, along with Art of Fighting's resident ninja Eiji Kisaragi (last seen in KOF95), and aikido devotee Kasumi (from KOF96's womens' team); and endboss Omega Rugal is joined by 96's infamously cheap Goenitz and a newly renovated version of Orochi, the skinny-jeans wearing snake god from KOF97.

Make no mistake; aside from the obvious exclusion of the boss characters, all the new characters in 98 UM are balanced to fit in with the rest of the cast, which itself has had some tweaks, both major and minor, to make them play just a bit differently from the original version.  WIth the Final Edition, further rebalancing attempts were made to ensure that all 59(!) characters are viable, with some underappreciated characters (such as Lucky Glauber) getting a much-needed boost in effectiveness.

If I had any complaints about this PC port, it's that I wish it had a couple of the extra features from the PS2 version of KOF98UM, like the single-player challenges and palette editor.  As it is, it's a straight port of the 2009 release on Xbox 360, with some brand new balance tweaks.  Those are pretty minor omissions, however, and for the price tag, you're getting a good deal nonetheless.

As others have said, this is indeed the Final Edition of King of Fighters 98UM. However, that means it's the final rebalancing. It doesn't include the features the PS2 one does because that's not the version that was ported. It's a port of the XBLA version with all the balance changes applied to it. It's about as close to arcade perfect as you'll get. I can understand why people would be disappointed by that, but all things considered this is a good port. Now let's talk about the part everybody cares about most.

The netcode itself seems to be about KoFXIII's levels of quality. So it's very playable, but not perfect. This has been my experience with player matches only with players ranging from 100ms to 200ms. Yes, it displays the ping times, thank God. When someone's connection has issues, you can definitely feel the delay, but it resyncs pretty quickly.

Single player consists of small challenges, arcade mode, 1v1 matches, etc. All the stuff you would expect from a fighter. It also includes the NeoGeo version of KoF98 if you want to play that.

So to sum it up: few SP modes, no PS2 features, only way to play FE outside of arcades, netcode is good for input delay based netcode. So you're getting an arcade faithful version of KoF98UM FE with online play. I'm happy with it, but you can't please everybody. One little thing I'm personally happy about is that everybody is unlocked from the start, too.

EDIT: Rollback netcode has been added; disregard the previous impressions. Buy without hesitation if online play is the deciding factor.

This is probably my favorite video game in existence, but I'm probably biased. The King of Fighters 94 was one of the earliest fighting games I was exposed to, and I quickly fell in love with the franchise.

Both 98 Ultimate Match and 2002 Ultimate Match represent the two pinnacles of the franchise. No other KOF exceeds those two (not 13, and definitely not 14). For me, it's often a toss-up between 98 and 2002, as to which one is truly the best.

98, in my opinion, offers a nearly perfect balance between complexity and simplicity. Without some of the more wild mechanics of 2002 (which I do enjoy), 98 offers the purest form of KOF there is, with the only the best mechanics and best characters KOF has to offer (except Xiangfei).

If you've never played KOF before, get this game, and this game first, since it's either best or second best depending on where the coin lands, and it's one of the simpler ones. If you have played KOF and still don't own this game, well, that would be a bit embarrassing, so don't dawdle.

The King of Fighters '98 is one of the best fighting games and a great example of when they do everything right. Released right after a "chapter closure", the game follows no storyline (like Real Bout Fatal Fury Special, KOF 2002 and Tekken Tag Tournament), so for once the developers don't have a chance to throw us a lot of bullshit and mess around with the characters list, they just deliver a package of their best work so far.

10/10 and be sure to check out The King of Fighters 2002 Unlimited Match, another SNK masterpiece.

The Ultimate Match edition of King of Fighters '98 is the best in home experience that you can have with this fighter outside of buying a Neo Geo. The roster is rather large and includes a good number of exclusive characters, so you'll have a lot of teams to experiment to your liking. While I feel that the series started strongly at '94, '98 is the first King of Fighters that I felt become the powerhouse that most players remember today, with a robust yet easy to pick up system and the presentation and art having a dramatic lift from previous iterations. It also adopted the Dream Match mainstay, expanding from SNK series like Fatal Fury and Art of Fighting, while deliving deeper into more obscure franchises like Psycho Soldier and Ikari Warriors. This version also has the updated Ultimate Match that has returning cast like Geese Howard while also giving the option of playing a Neo Geo rom of the original version of The King of Fighters '98 for the purists.

The only issue is a mainstay in most SNK ports, being that the netplay is bad. While the connections are up in the air, it's hard to even find a decent match online. Sadly, there is not a large community currently available, so unless you have a group of friends, it's best to go in expecting not to get much mileage out of the online play.

Nearly 2 decades later, The King of Fighters '98 still holds up as a very competant fighter and is enjoyable to go back to every now and then. While I recommend The King of Fighters XIII as the best overall representation and evolution of the series, '98 is still a very well made game and worth checking out to see the roots of SNK's most well known fighting franchise.

It's KoF 98 with a bunch of options and many settings & modes to find something your pace or play style.  Definitely a must for your library if you're into fighting games at all (and obviously a recommendation for KoF fans).

I might not be able to speak for everyone else, but KoF '98, along with this update, is what got me more into fighting games. There's such a delightfully large variety among the cast of characters, whether it's ease of use, skill cap, playstyle, or personality that it's really hard to not like at least a couple of them. There are so many ways to fine-tune your playstyle and mess around with different options, e.g. ordering your characters in different ways or hand-picking the different Advanced or Extra options, that you can really find something that works for you or use stuff way differently than it was intended and still have fun. What's really important, however, is that the game doesn't present it all up-front so as to intimidate newer players. It's all pretty smoothly integrated into the regular gameplay, with the exception of typical fighting game shenanigans like memorizing special moves and such. The game is excellent at really making you feel comfortable with the mechanics and cast and really lets you experiment until you find something that fits you just right, and it's because of this that I recommend it to anyone who might be interested in fighting games. Simple enough and with a wide enough breadth of content on a surface level to draw anyone in, fighting game player or not, yet technically complex and demanding enough to keep veterans interested for a very long time.

INTRO: A BRIEF HISTORY OF KOF 98

KOF 98 at its first release quickly became one of SNK's biggest blockbusters in the arcades. Having just wrapped up their first significant story arc, the Orochi Saga, in 97, SNK decided to make their first Dream Match game, where the cast was not bound by any canon restrictions. As a refinement upon gameplay concepts explored in KOF 97 and featuring characters who had died during the Orochi Saga, 98 was received with open arms.

In the years that followed, KOF 98 stood as a legend in fighting games and remained one of the pinnacles of KOF. Through new KOF entries and even SNK's own demise, 98 remained a constant in the KOF community and still has strong widespread communities today.

To celebrate the 10 year anniversary, SNK released a remake in KOF 98 Ultimate Match, where a lot of positive changes were made to the original, including the rework of the previously weak and gimmicky Extra mode, and cool new characters were added. 98UM brought back the '96 boss team (Geese Howard, Wolfgang Krauser, and Mr. Big) as well as Kasumi and Eiji. In addition to these, 4 new EX characters were added (EX Blue Mary, EX Yamazaki, EX Geese, and EX King: the former three being based on their appearances in Real Bout Fatal Fury 2, while EX King being based off her Art of Fighting appearance).

These 9 additional characters round out the cast to a whopping 59!

However, there were some significant balance problems that plagued it, the most infamous of which being Krauser's dominance: his overwhelming strength was enough for him to end up on the teams for most players. After Tougeki 2008, KOF 98UM had lost a lot of popularity. Most in the 98 community preferred the original to the Krauser fest.

A couple years later in 2010, a new revolution in the arcade industry was introduced in the form of NESiCAxLive, an online distribution service for arcade games ran by Taito. SNK Playmore chose to release 98UM and 02UM on the service. 02UM already having been an amazing success for them, they wanted 98UM to attain similar success. And here is where we get to...


KOF 98 UM [FINAL EDITION]

For KOF 98 UM's NESiCA release, SNK Playmore decided to update 98UM. This update brings about a host of balance changes (great list compiled here http://dreamcancel.com/wiki/index.php?title=King_of_Fighters_98UM_Final_Edition) to fix the problems of the first 98UM. With the exception of Krauser receiving a host of nerfs and touches to Iori's command grab and Eiji's MAX projectile super, the entire cast received buffs and/or quality of life changes, and certain system mechanics were standardized (Extra meter charge times, charge motion input times).

It's absolutely astounding how well refined the balance became. EVERYONE is strong, EVERYONE is a threat. The tier list is SUPER compressed as a result of how viable everyone in the game is. Everyone has fun and interesting tools. Honestly this may be the closest to perfection humanity may see in this lifetime.

So yeah this game is fucking amazing on the gameplay end of things, but let's take a look at this port finally.

3 years of thinking we may never get this game, and it finally comes.




TECHNICAL REVIEW

This is a pretty solid port, but unfortunately not quite as incredible as the game itself is. Code Mystics ported over the 360 version of the game and implemented the Final Edition balance changes with new netcode. WHAT DOES THIS MEAN?!?!?

Well unfortunately that means this version doesn't include certain features from the PS2 version.

-No 3D stages (your mileage may vary, I don't like these very much personally)
-No arranged music (easily modded in if you look at the guides, but not having options is the slightest touch annoying)
-NO COLOR EDIT (this I'm actually really tight about. It's probably possible to mod the color palletes in the game but UUUUUUUUUUUGH)

All the other stuff is there though, and the game runs really well. The button config is also way better than the 360 version as not only can you just select the button you want to configure and hit your button, BUT YOU CAN TEST YOUR BUTTONS IN THE MENU. No more menuing through all those buttons and being utterly confused as to which buttons on your nonstandard controller/stick are which!

Code Mystics was also REALLY COOL and patched in options to see your inputs in training mode! No frame counter on it but still cool.


ONLINE

Online multiplayer is basically a requirement these days, aaaaaaaaand that 360 version's online was really really bad. How's this version? Not ideal unfortunately, but servicable enough in some cases I guess?

Despite GGPO's revolutionary rollback netcode implementation being a tried and true method, having cultivated large communities together for older games, it's unfortunately not here. Instead using the clearly outdated method of just adding input delay to compensate for lag.

This leaves me to address something that's outside the scope of this port.



THE COMMUNITY

One of things that curses 98UMFE is that the only platforms it's been released on are Steam and NESiCA. This ends up actually limiting some of the outreach this game can get as

1. NESiCA isn't the most widely spread arcade platform. A lot of KOF tournaments for older games are held on the original boards they came out on, including 02UM.

2. Steam (and PC in general honestly) isn't the most popular platform for tournaments in general. Most games utilize consoles or arcade boards where applicable.

It'd be really cool if 98UMFE was released on MORE platforms so it could hopefully get more exposure.

KoF98 is one of my favorite games and while UM is mostly the same game, I still consider vanilla 98, which is easily playable on fightcade, is the superior experience.

PROS (compared to vanilla):
Larger roster with more color choices
Characters that were decidedly weak in vanilla were appropriately buffed; overpowered characters were given reasonable nerfs
Random elements removed (damage, stun, smiley, teammates interrupting certain grabs and combos during stun)
Engine slowdown has been completely removed
EXTRA mode can no longer spam supers when the player's health as low due to a cooldown
EXTRA mode gives the player a faster walk in exchange for the inability to run
ULTIMATE mode allows you to mix and match ADVANCE and EXTRA system mechanics

CON (singular) (compared to vanilla):
EXTRA Mode players are able to tech throws - one of the biggest hurdles new/intermediate players have to overcome is learning how to punish bad rolls; the easy solution is usually to throw the opponent during the roll, but the opponent is able to tech during their roll, so this simply doesn't work against anyone choosing to abuse throws. You therefore have to learn to punish the roll during the vulnerability frames after the roll with a meaty attack or a command grab. Unlike rolls however, spot dodges do NOT have vulnerability frames, they can be spammed without consequence if you are not using a character with a command grab. The player spamming dodges still has to be careful to not use the dodge's followup attack to avoid being punished, but this puts way more of the onus on the attacker to punish the defender's poor decision-making. Of all the the changes made to 98, this is easily the most egregious and the core reason I consider vanilla the better game overall.

It's still KoF98, it's a still a great game, just know it's not a straight upgrade to the original, go play it.

[h1]The Short[/h1]
[i]A controller with a stick, such as your standard dualshock style, is highly recommended for this game.[/i]

[i]King of Fighters '98[/i] is a fighting game that was released into arcades and for the Neo Geo in—when else?—1998, a whopping two decades ago now.  This [i][u]Ultimate Match Final Edition[/u][/i] is an updated re-release whose primary change is the addition of more characters and gameplay modes.  The original release was always a superb game, quite well remembered in the history of fighting games, and this update does nothing to detract from that original glow.  It brings all the updates you could [i]want[/i] to first release.

For even a casual fan of fighting games, this is a great selection.  It's polished in gameplay, has an expansive and diverse roster, and is memorable to the last punch.

[h1]The Long[/h1]
King of Fighters is a classic 2D fighter in the vein of the more well known [i]Street Fighter[/i].  The big innovation KOF brought to the genre, in its time, was [b]team battles[/b]: instead of selecting [b]one[/b] character and fighting best two out of three rounds against another character, you pick [b]three[/b] characters and select an order for them, and they fight knockout style in one-on-one rounds until all the opponents are exhausted (or until your team is).  As is typical, every character comes equipped with your standard punches and kicks and then also a set of command-input special moves and super moves (lists of the command inputs are provided in-game for you), and the game itself has a few basic battle mechanics which are easy to use but difficult to master, such as dodging, move canceling, and so on.

Picking teams immediately encourages learning multiple characters, which the game provides in droves.  There are [b]forty-five[/b] character tiles available on the selection screen but, even better, several characters have [i]alternate versions[/i] hidden under their tiles which you can access by holding the select button.  Most of the alternate versions are the same character with an adjusted movelist taken from some prior game appearance.  Counting the alternates as unique selections brings the roster up to [b]sixty-four[/b].  [i]Every last character[/i] from the first four KOF games is included, which is a nice upgrade from the original release which, though it had many characters, was always missing just a handful.  Nothing needs to be unlocked either; it's all available to you right out of the gate.

Primary gameplays modes are [b]Arcade Mode[/b] (7 stages, including the one-of-three final bosses), [b]Vs Mode[/b] (against human or CPU), [b]Single Mode[/b] (Arcade Mode à la Street Fighter instead of team matches), [b]Vs Single Mode[/b], and [b]Endless Mode[/b] (not literally; you pick one character and fight all sixty-four other characters one at a time).  There are a few [b]Challenges[/b] available as well, which are mostly an excuse to practice the game's mechanics.  The original Arcade/Neo Geo release is also included and selectable from the main menu, missing characters and all, as a bonus for the purists and historians amongst us.

The music is a [i]"Best Of"[/i] from the prior KOF games, and it's a great soundtrack to fight to.  There are themes associated with every team, some themes associated with specific characters, and even occasionally themes for specific match-ups.

There's no story component to the game.  The history of such is that all four prior KOF games had an ongoing storyline which resolved in KOF '97.  So the '98 release was a celebratory party game with no story, just lots of past characters.

In flaws, this game only has small nitpicks:
[list][*]There's no fast-reset option, so if need to get back to the main menu then you always have to get [i]into[/i] an active match before you can finally quit to the menu.
[*]At the end of a round the screen clutters with some extra information, occasionally blocking your view of a character's victory pose.
[*]Though movelists are provided, the game does very little to explain its mechanics and you're left to know them from past experience or to look them up online.
[*]The way Arcade Mode is set up means there's a whole block of characters you [i]almost never[/i] fight, and a few which you [i]constantly[/i] fight, which is a little disappointing for a game with such a large cast.
[*]Like many fighting games of this nature, the difficulty setting is a little finicky.  Some CPU-controlled characters are inherently more difficult than others, the CPU occasionally enjoys bouts of precognitive intuition, and so forth.  Even on a fixed difficulty setting you'll get CPUs who brutally go ham on your ass alongside polite ones who will lift very few fingers to defend themselves, and even on the single character level it's inconsistent when the CPU will be drunk or go into a trance of ultimate fighting zen.  Here as everywhere else, battling a human player is a test of [i]skill[/i] and battlng the CPU is a test of [i]smarts[/i].[/list]
All the flaws are minor things like that, some of which are simply the things you can't escape if you're playing fighting games.

All of them together don't nearly tarnish the shining excellence of this game.  For fighting games, it's a premier example of the genre.  This is one to collect for dedicated fighter fans, but also a fantastic choice for someone looking to get into fighters on even a basic level, or to get into the KOF universe.  I've known KOF '98 for almost two decades now, and I'm still coming back to it.

THE KING OF FIGHTERS ’98 ULTIMATE MATCH FINAL EDITION on Steam represents a rare example of a fighting game that has not only endured but continued to thrive decades after its original release. Developed by SNK CORPORATION with modernization support from Code Mystics and published by SNK CORPORATION, this edition proudly honors the legacy of the franchise while updating it just enough to meet contemporary expectations. KOF ’98 has long been regarded as the series’ most refined and beloved entry, often referred to as “The Dream Match” thanks to its roster and absence of strict narrative continuity, and this definitive version ensures that legacy remains accessible to both longtime fans and new players discovering it for the first time. Instead of overhauling mechanics or presentation, the developers wisely chose to preserve the original’s pacing, structure, and competitive identity, creating a version that feels authentic rather than reconstructed.

At its core, the game remains a pure expression of traditional 2D fighting design—fast, technical, and deeply strategic without sacrificing personality or approachability. The four-button control scheme is deceptively simple, enabling players to ease into the fundamentals without feeling overwhelmed, yet beneath that lies a vast layer of nuance defined by hops, rolls, cancels, blowback attacks, guard mechanics, conditioning, and spacing battles. Movement is central to the experience, and mastering the timing of short hops and hyper hops becomes just as important as executing special moves or combos. Unlike many modern fighters that lean into long strings and cinematic execution, KOF ’98 prioritizes neutral footsies, reads, and momentum shifts. The three-character team system deepens this even further, encouraging players to think about order selection, matchup advantages, and meter distribution across the full duration of a fight.

The roster remains one of the game’s greatest strengths and a major reason it continues to be played competitively. With more than 60 playable characters, the selection spans multiple SNK franchises and eras, offering everything from established tournament staples like Kyo, Terry, Iori, and Chizuru to more experimental fighters with unusual toolkits. Each character feels handcrafted, with distinctive normals, movement speeds, specials, mix-up options, and combo opportunities that reflect a specific fighting philosophy. What stands out, especially compared to other retro fighters, is the surprising level of balance. While tiers exist, the majority of the cast remains viable, and skilled players can succeed with personal favorites rather than being forced into a narrow meta. The choice between Advanced and Extra playstyles allows players to tailor their strategy further, providing different approaches to meter building, defensive options, and offensive pressure.

Code Mystics’ enhancements elevate this edition beyond a simple port, ensuring its longevity in an online-driven era. The implementation of rollback netcode is transformative, allowing smooth online matches across long distances, something essential for a competitive fighter built on precise timing and tight neutral engagements. Online lobbies, ranked matchmaking, spectator functionality, and multiple connection customization options show a clear dedication to community-driven play. The training mode has also been expanded to facilitate lab work, testing combos, punishes, setups, and defensive responses. Importantly, none of these improvements interfere with the original mechanics, animations, game speed, or timing windows—elements competitive players depend on remaining consistent.

Visually, the game exudes retro charm without feeling dated. SNK’s sprite work remains expressive, kinetic, and full of personality, achieving clarity and animation quality that many modern pixel-art games still struggle to match. Character animations convey weight, intent, and emotional flair, making every punch, throw, fireball, and anti-air feel distinct. Stages showcase a variety of international settings, each filled with colorful crowds, atmospheric details, and memorable musical themes. The soundtrack is equally timeless, mixing rock, jazz, synth, and orchestral influences into energetic battle themes that still resonate with players decades later. Together, the visuals and music create a competitive atmosphere that feels energetic without overwhelming the senses, allowing concentration while still delivering excitement.

As polished and feature-rich as this edition is, it remains a product of its era, and those qualities may not resonate with every player. The game offers little in the way of narrative presentation, cinematic flair, or single-player depth—its arcade mode serves as a traditional endurance ladder rather than a story-driven campaign. Tutorials remain minimal, requiring newcomers to research techniques such as option-selects, safe jumps, hop pressure, buffering, and character-specific combos. Some older roster quirks and matchup imbalances persist, especially at the highest level of play. Yet for many fans, these elements contribute to its authenticity rather than diminishing it, reinforcing the game’s identity as a competitive-focused fighter grounded in skill development and long-term mastery.

Ultimately, THE KING OF FIGHTERS ’98 ULTIMATE MATCH FINAL EDITION is more than a historical re-release—it is an active competitive platform, a celebration of SNK’s fighting legacy, and a testament to how well-crafted mechanics can outlast technological trends. Its fluid combat, massive roster, balanced systems, and intense neutral game continue to draw players who appreciate depth earned through practice rather than shortcuts. For returning veterans, it serves as the definitive way to revisit a foundational classic. For genre newcomers, it offers an opportunity to experience one of the most influential and enduring fighting games ever made. Few titles maintain relevance for over 25 years, yet this one not only survives—it continues to thrive, proving why many still regard it as the pinnacle of 2D team-based fighting design.

[h1]Great game. Great remake. Disappointing port.[/h1]
KOF 98 was one of the greatest games in The King of Fighters franchise. And when KOF 98 Ultimate Match first came out in consoles, it has major improvements compared to the original, including ALL the characters from KOF 94 to KOF 97. Unfortunately, the Steam port is a crippled version of the console versions, especially regarding visuals and music. While in the PlayStation2 version you could choose between the classic 2D and re-vamped 3D stages, and between the original soundtrack from the NeoGeo arcades and the arranged soundtrack that played in the original console ports, the Steam version comes only with 2D stages, and the NeoGeo's OST. No options to choose 3D stages or arranged music at all. This was a disappointment to me. Overall, the game itself still retains most of the original's essence, but it lacks features the console versions had.
And in my opinion, some of the arranged versions of the soundtrack are FAR SUPERIOR to the NeoGeo tracks.
